newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis talks hit lull amid calls for probe.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis talks hit lull amid calls for probe.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels were set on Wednesday to take a break from hostage talks amid growing optimism, while opposition lawmakers called for a congressional probe into the 2 1/2-month crisis.
Wrapping up a sixth round of preliminary talks on Tuesday, Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels and government negotiators agreed to skip a day and hold a seventh meeting on Thursday.
No details of Tuesday's discussions were given, but Peruvian and Japanese officials were upbeat about progress in the talks to end the 71-day drama at the Japanese ambassador's Lima mansion.

"We are optimistic because, since the direct intervention of the MRTA chief, we are in more direct conversations," Congress President Victor Joy Way, a pro-government lawmaker, told local radio on Tuesday.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Wednesday told reporters: "As with the previous session, it seems to have been conducted in a very good atmosphere. They may be starting work to sort out points of agreement and differences."

After Tuesday's three-hour meeting, rebel leader Nestor Cerpa and his second-in-command Rolly Rojas were driven from a Red Cross safe house where talks are held back across the street to the besieged residence.

"The talks have continued in the same atmosphere as the previous meetings," Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, representing the Vatican as one of three guarantors mediating in the crisis, told reporters in a statement.
The guarantors, who are sworn to secrecy, described earlier meetings as taking place "in a constructive atmosphere."

Opposition lawmakers, meanwhile, said Congress should investigate why Peru's police and intelligence service failed to prevent a band of heavily armed rebels from storming the diplomatic compound on Dec. 17, seizing hundreds of VIPs.
They continue to hold 72 mostly middle-aged men in what has become Latin America's longest hostage siege.
"We are going to propose an exhaustive investigation," Congressman Fernando Olivera of the Independent Moralizing Front (FIM) party told local television late on Tuesday.
But Congress is dominated by President Alberto Fujimori's New Majority-Change 90 party and pro-government lawmakers said it was not the right time to try to affix blame.
"We have to wait until this is over and at that moment determine exactly who are responsible," said Ricardo Marcenaro of New Majority-Change 90.

As talks to bloodlessly end the siege drag on, word on the state of the hostages and their captors has come from a source close to medical teams which regularly enter the residence to provide check-ups. The source said Cerpa's mood was darkening.
"Cerpa looks irritated. He doesn't speak with everyone any more," the source, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

While Cerpa was increasingly morose, the hostages -- especially Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki and Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela -- were cheerful when the doctors entered the residence last Thursday.

"There is an atmosphere of optimism inside the residence. Some of them play chess, card games, ludo, and others read books so as not to be bored as they wait for whatever is going to happen," said the source.
The hostages were mostly in good health. But two need to have medicines brought in from the outside for serious illnesses. The doctors also examine rebels if they request it.

"Once, two of the MRTA women asked the doctors, half-joking but half-seriously, if they could do a scan to see if they were pregnant," the source said. "Anyway, they did the tests and they were negative."
